In the UK, Ofcom requires the World Cup to be listed as a 'Listed Sporting Event', meaning in theory all World Cup matches must be broadcast free-to-air on terrestrial television, while the two broadcasters BBC and ITV do not air advertisements during the drinks breaks. China's National Radio and Television Administration stipulates that broadcasting rights for the World Cup, Asian Games and Olympics must be monopolised by CCTV, which at the last minute secured the rights for this tournament from FIFA at a relatively low price in recent years.

PCCW wins broadcast rights for third consecutive term, with per capita cost ranking among the world's highest

Back in Hong Kong, PCCW, which holds licences for both free-to-air and pay-TV as well as fixed-line and mobile telecommunications, has secured the broadcast rights for three consecutive tournaments. In contrast, after TVB suffered losses from broadcasting the World Cup and Cable TV shut down its pay-TV service, there are no bidders in the market with cross-platform and bundled sales advantages.

FIFA is also believed to have gauged the 'cutting the cord' pressure PCCW faces in customer retention, charging Hong Kong a certain broadcast fee. The exclusive Hong Kong broadcast rights for this World Cup are reportedly sold for HK$170 million, slightly lower than previous editions, yet on a per capita basis Hong Kong still ranks among the world's highest. Although the 'pass' fee for watching World Cup matches has not increased this time, and restaurants and eateries have joined in broadcasting, along with the 'online football commentary craze' giving fans more options, a return to the era of the World Cup being 'shared by all' remains a distant prospect.

Commercial sponsors shape the rules of the game, not just 'watching the match and incidentally the sneakers'

During the World Cup, from pitch-side advertising to VAR, everything represents a golden opportunity to capture viewers' attention, making it easy to understand why commercial sponsorship and licensing are another important revenue source for FIFA. FIFA divides sponsors mainly into four tiers, with sponsors worldwide secretly competing for global influence every four years.

The stable top-tier FIFA Partners in recent editions are all globally renowned brands, including Adidas, Coca-Cola, Hyundai and Visa. Partners also include potential host nations; for example, Qatar Airways has been a sponsor since 2017, and Saudi Aramco, the oil company of Saudi Arabia which will host the 2034 World Cup, has also joined as a sponsor from this edition onwards, in an open transaction with FIFA.

Chinese sponsors, who have gained attention with Chinese-language advertising slogans in recent years, have seen their sponsorship amounts for this edition drop by nearly 70 percent. Wanda, which was a top-tier partner in the previous two editions, was removed for owing sponsorship fees, exiting alongside mobile phone brand Vivo from the same period. The remaining major Chinese sponsors include Lenovo and Hisense, which respectively hold naming rights for the newly introduced 'Referee Cam' and VAR display equipment, as well as Mengniu, which frequently appears with the baffling slogan 'If you can't drink milk, try soft milk'.

Haaland endorses Wong Lo Kat, Messi features in Mengniu advertisement

Time zone differences for matches and China-US relations may affect Chinese companies' willingness to sponsor, but Chinese firms may have realised that endorsements could be more effective than mere brand exposure. The example is the heated online discussion about Norwegian striker Haaland's Wong Lo Kat herbal tea advertisement. French star Mbappé endorses 'Bu Shui La', an electrolyte drink under Dongpeng Beverage, which was listed in Hong Kong with much fanfare this year, with the ad deliberately aired during the drinks break. Spanish forward Lamine Yamal and Argentine king of football Messi also appear alongside Mengniu in this edition's advertisements. When world-class footballers' endorsement ads incorporate 'Chinese characteristics', they are often seen as awkward, but for Chinese companies, this contrast represents a traffic code.

Changes in World Cup sponsors are also reshaping the form of the tournament. Although American domestic brands such as Bank of America, telecom company Verizon, and Frito-Lay, the parent company of Lay's potato chips, have successively joined, local host-nation sponsorships are often short-lived. As for Japanese electronics companies, which were once regular World Cup sponsors fading from the pitch, speculated to be a signal of Japan's economic recession, in fact many of them have shifted to commercial markets with higher profit margins than consumer electronics, lacking incentive to pursue global exposure.

All non-sponsor brands banned inside venues

In recent World Cup editions, the scene of Chinese sponsors rallying pitch-side may in future not be replaced by another emerging nation, but rather gradually by ambush marketing lurking outside the venue. FIFA, citing the protection of sponsor interests, strictly enforces 'Clean Stadium' measures, banning all non-sponsor brands inside the venue. For example, Levi's Stadium, one of this edition's host venues, was temporarily renamed San Francisco Bay Area Stadium, with the jeans brand's giant logo inside covered by white cloth, and condiments brand logos inside covered with black tape. But brands such as Levi's and Heinz turned the ban into a marketing opportunity. FIFA and sponsors' tight defence is gradually bypassed by other brands one by one, forcing a tactical reshuffle.
